topics.title: The vault file

runs.s: Everything in a vault lives in one encrypted file, a .wmvault file. Without a way in, it is random-looking bytes of a fixed shape.
Because the file holds nothing readable, it can be copied anywhere: a backup folder, a cloud drive, a server you do not trust. Whoever holds a copy still needs a way in.

The items are encrypted under a random vault key. Each way in, such as a password, a password with a key file, or a password with a security key, opens a slot that holds a copy of that key. Changing a password rewraps the key and leaves the items as they are.
The file has room for eight ways in. Unused slots are random bytes, so nobody can tell from the file how many ways in it has, or whether one of them is a duress password.

A password is turned into a key with Argon2id, using at least 64 MiB of memory, and WM Pass refuses a file that asks for less. That makes every guess slow for someone trying passwords against a stolen copy.

The contents are padded and sealed in chunks, with a fresh key on every save, so the file's size says little and a cut or rearranged file fails to open. Each save also raises a counter inside the file, so an older copy can be told from a newer one.
Attachments are separate files, each under its own key, which is kept inside its item. Deleting the item for good destroys that key, and the attachment with it.
Decoy vaults sit beside the real one as files of the same shape. One password is tried against all of them in the time one file takes, so how long unlocking takes gives nothing away.
Anyone with a copy of the file and any of its ways in can read the whole vault.
Rekeying
protects what you write afterwards, not copies made before.
A vault saved by a newer version of WM Pass may open read-only in an older one, so that saving cannot drop fields the older version does not know.
The format is published on the WM Pass website. No outside audit of the core has been done yet.

topics.title: The master password

runs.s: The password that opens your vault. It unlocks the key to everything in it, and nobody can reset it.
There is no account and no server that holds a copy, so there is no reset link. That is also what keeps anyone else, WM Pass included, from opening your vault.
When you make a vault, the door shows how hard the password would be to guess, and
Create vault
stays off until it is strong enough.
Generate a passphrase
suggests five random words.
Unlocking turns the password into a key slowly on purpose, so that every guess is slow for anyone trying passwords against a copy of the file.
After five wrong tries in a row, the door makes you wait: 30 seconds at first, doubling each time up to 15 minutes.
You can add more passwords that open the same vault, and require a key file or a security key alongside one. See
A good one is long, random, and used nowhere else. Four or five random words work well, and are easier to type than a jumble of symbols. Keep a written copy somewhere safe until you know it by heart.
Forget it and the vault is gone, unless you have another way in or made an
emergency kit
The waits apply at this door only. Someone who copies the file can guess elsewhere, slowed only by the key derivation, which is why the password's strength matters.
A new password does not change what older backups open with. See

topics.title: Kinds of item

runs.s: A vault holds twelve kinds of item. Each has the fields that kind of thing needs, and all of them share the same extras.

items.s: A login holds a username and password, with the websites it is for, a one-time code, passkeys, an email alias and security questions.
A code is a one-time code on its own, for an account whose password is kept elsewhere.
A note is text kept secret until you open it.
A card has the name on it, its number, expiry, security code, PIN, issuer and billing address.
An identity has a full name, email, phone, address and date of birth.
A recovery item keeps a recovery phrase or a list of backup codes, and the account it is for.
A Wi-Fi item has the network name, its security, the password, and whether the network is hidden.
An SSH key has the private and public key, fingerprint and passphrase, and says whether the SSH agent on a computer may offer it.
An API key has its provider, key, secret, scopes and expiry date.
A database item has the engine, host, port, database name, user and password, whether to use TLS, and a connection string.
A license has the product, license key, who it is licensed to, order number and expiry date.
A document has its type and number, with the scans as attachments.

runs.s: Every kind can also have a folder, tags, a color and icon, notes, fields of your own, attachments, links to other items, a reminder and a self-destruct date. Old values of its secret fields are kept in its history.
Secret fields, such as passwords, card numbers, keys and notes, stay hidden until you choose to see them, and search leaves them alone.
Pick the kind that matches the thing, so its fields and copy buttons fit. Use
Code
when only the one-time code belongs in WM Pass; when the password is here too, keep the code in the login, so one item has both.
Which kinds the add menu offers, and in what order, is up to you under

topics.title: Searching the vault

runs.s: The search box finds items across the whole vault by their name, websites, username and other plain fields. A few extra words narrow it down.
Type part of a name. Words of four letters or more also match with a letter or two missing, so "gthub" still finds GitHub.

Search looks at names, websites, tags, usernames, the holder and issuer of cards, names and emails on identities, database hosts and users, Wi-Fi names, products, providers, and the names of fields you added. It never looks inside a password or another secret.
These words narrow a search, and can be combined:

items.s: "tag:work", "kind:card", "site:github" and "folder:bank" keep to one tag, kind, website or folder. "kind:" takes login, otp, note, card, identity, recovery, wifi, ssh, api, database, license or document.
"has:otp", "has:passkey", "has:attachment", "has:alias", "has:notes", "has:link", "has:history" and "has:reminder" keep the items that have one.
"weak", "reused", "breached", "old" and "duplicate" keep the items the health check flags, and "pinned" and "favorite" keep those.
"modified<30d" keeps items changed in the last 30 days, and "modified>1y" those not changed for a year. "created<" and "created>" work the same way. Use d, w, m or y.
A word starting with a minus, such as "-old", leaves out items that match it. Quotes keep words together.
"in:notes" looks inside notes as well, which search otherwise leaves alone.

runs.s: Items in the trash and on the hidden shelf stay out of results. "trashed" brings the trash in, and "hidden" brings in the shelf while it is open.
Best matches come first, with pinned items at the top. Before you type, the search page offers words to start from under
Look for
, such as
Weak
Has code
and
Changed recently
, with the items you opened last below them.
Tap the search bar on the Vault tab. If nothing matches, the search page offers to add what you typed as a new login.
The word "breached" finds only what a breach check found since the vault was last unlocked. See
Search leaves passwords and other secrets alone on purpose: a search box must not become a way to test what a password is.

topics.title: Locking

runs.s: Locking closes the vault and wipes its key from memory. Until you unlock it again, WM Pass can show, copy or fill nothing from it.
An open vault is readable by anyone at the keyboard. Locking often, and by itself, keeps that window short.
Before it locks, WM Pass saves any change still waiting and leaves a nested vault you were in. The key is then wiped from memory, and the hidden shelf closes.
It locks when you tap the lock button, this long after you leave the app under
, when the screen goes off if
is on, and when a panic app signals it.

Getting back in takes the master password, or your fingerprint if you turned that on. The fingerprint key lives in the phone's secure hardware, and a fingerprint added to the phone later makes it unusable, so you type the password again.
Lock whenever you step away. The timer is a safety net for the times you forget.
Locking does not protect a vault from a program that was already running on the computer while it was open.
Locking does not empty the clipboard. A secret copied before the lock keeps its own timer. See

topics.title: Copying secrets

runs.s: When you copy a password, a code or another secret, WM Pass marks it as sensitive and empties the clipboard again after a while.
Anything on the clipboard can be read by other programs and pasted by mistake into the wrong place. Marking a copy and clearing it soon after narrows both.
A copied secret is marked as sensitive, so Android keeps it out of clipboard previews and history where it honors the mark.
A small bar counts down until it is cleared, with
Clear now
When the time set under
is up, WM Pass empties the clipboard, unless you have copied something else since.
If WM Keyboard is your keyboard, its clipboard history keeps the copy only until then: when WM Pass empties the clipboard, the keyboard drops it from its history too.
Usernames, websites and other plain fields are copied as they are, and not cleared.
Where you can, fill instead of copying: the autofill service does not use the clipboard.
A program reading the clipboard during those seconds still sees the secret.
Locking the vault does not clear the clipboard early.

topics.plain: When you copy a password, a code or another secret, WM Pass marks it as sensitive and empties the clipboard again after a while.

topics.title: The hidden shelf

runs.s: A place for items you do not want seen by accident. Items on the shelf stay out of every list and search until you open the shelf with your master password.
Some items should not show when you open the vault in front of someone. The shelf keeps them out of the way without a second vault.
Open an item and, under
More
at the bottom, choose
Move to hidden shelf
To see them, open Settings, Hidden shelf, and type your master password. It is asked even though the vault is already open.
While the shelf is open, its items open and edit as usual. Tap
Close the shelf
, or lock the vault, and they go out of sight again.
Open or closed, shelf items are never offered for autofill and never shown on the Codes tab.
For a few items you would rather keep out of sight. For a whole separate set of items, a
nested vault
or a
decoy vault
fits better.
The shelf hides items. It does not encrypt them separately: they are in the same vault file, under the same key, and anyone who has the master password can open the shelf.
Shelf items still count towards the health score.
Backups and sync carry shelf items like any other, since they copy the whole file.

topics.title: Duress and decoys

runs.s: Passwords that do something other than open your vault, for when someone makes you unlock it. At the door they look exactly like any other password.
Refusing is not always safe. A duress password lets you appear to give in while protecting what matters.

Each way into the vault fills a slot in the file, and the slot says what happens when its password is typed: open the vault, wipe this device's copy, or lock hard. Slots are sealed and unused ones are random, so nobody can read from the file which kind a password is, or how many there are.

items.s: A
erases the vault on this phone and shows "Wrong password." WM Pass also forgets the backup places, accounts and paired devices it knew here.
A
refuses every password for an hour, the right one included. Nothing is lost.
A
is a separate vault with its own password. Fill it with a few believable logins, so it holds up to a look.
A panic app such as Ripple can tell WM Pass to lock, or to wipe, as set under

runs.s: Two more things help: the
hidden shelf
keeps chosen items out of sight, and
Self-destruct
, under
More
on an item, removes it at a time you choose.
Set these up only if you might face someone you cannot refuse, and keep backups somewhere they cannot reach. Those backups are how you get the vault back after a wipe.

These help against a quick look under pressure. They do not defeat forensics: flash storage does not reliably erase, and a disk image taken earlier, or a sync provider's file history, still holds what it held.
A wipe touches only this device. Backups, synced copies and other devices keep the vault.
An item that has self-destructed still exists in any copy made before then.
Someone with an older copy of your files to compare against may notice a decoy.

topics.title: Emergency access

runs.s: A way for people you trust to open your vault together if you cannot, without any one of them being able to do it alone.
Nothing can recover a forgotten master password, and nobody can reach your vault if something happens to you. An emergency kit gives that power to a group, and to no single person.
The kit adds a recovery key to the vault as its own way in, then splits that key into shares. You choose how many people, from two to seven, and how many of them it takes.
Fewer than that number learn nothing at all from their shares, even if they put them together.
WM Pass saves the kit as a file. Print it, give each person their share, then delete the file.
To use it, enough of them take a copy of the vault file to WM Pass, choose
Add another vault or account
at the door, or
I already have a vault
on a new device, then
Recover with emergency shares
. They paste the shares, choose a new password, and the vault opens.
When there are people you would trust with the whole vault today. Choose how many it takes, such as any three of five, so one lost share or one absent person does not block the rest.
Nothing enforces a waiting period. People holding enough shares can open the vault at once, so any wait is a promise between you.
They also need a copy of the vault file, so make sure they can get one, from a backup for example.
Rekeying
stops the shares working. Make a new kit afterwards.
Someone holding enough shares and an old copy of the file can still read that old copy after you rekey.

topics.title: Working offline

runs.s: WM Pass works fully without a network, and nothing leaves the device until you turn on
Allow network features
. Each feature that needs the network says what it sends, and to whom, before it runs.
A password manager that talks to the internet is one more thing to trust. Staying local by default means the only copies of your vault are the ones you make.
One switch stands in front of every feature that reaches the internet. While it is off, a page that needs it says what it would send, with
Allow network features
to turn it on.
Setting up a backup place on a server, or adding a Bitwarden or server account, turns it on, since that is your yes to reaching it.
With it on, network features run when you use them. In the background, only what you set up runs, such as scheduled backups.

Web requests go over https. Plain http is refused, except to this device and to Tailscale addresses, where nothing readable crosses a network. SFTP, FTP, SMB, NFS and IMAP connections encrypt or not as the server and the place's settings decide.
Site icons come with the app, so showing them never tells anyone which sites are in your vault.
What each feature sends:

items.s: Breach checks: the first five characters of each password's SHA-1 hash to Have I Been Pwned, and an email address to the service you pick.
Email aliases: your API key and the note you write, to the forwarding service.
Disposable inbox: a request for a throwaway address, to a public mail service.
Username checker: the name, to each site it asks.
Backups and sync: the encrypted vault file, to the place you chose.
Accounts: sign-in and sync with Bitwarden, Vaultwarden or your own server. Your password itself is never sent.
Sync on your own network: encrypted traffic to your paired devices, with nothing in between.

runs.s: Leave it off if you use WM Pass on one device and keep backups in a folder. Turn it on when you want one of the features above.
Backups to a folder and opening a KeePass file need no network, so they work with this off.
The offline build of the app has no permission to reach a network at all, so these features are not in it. It cannot sync over your own network either, since Android counts that as internet access.

topics.plain: WM Pass works fully without a network, and nothing leaves the device until you turn on Allow network features. Each feature that needs the network says what it sends, and to whom, before it runs.

topics.title: Breach checks

runs.s: Checks whether your passwords, or the email addresses in your vault, appear in published leaks. It runs only when you ask.
A password that has leaked anywhere is on the lists attackers try first, however strong it looks. Knowing which ones have leaked tells you what to change first.
Check every password

goes through each item with a password. WM Pass hashes the password with SHA-1 and sends only the first five characters of the hash to Have I Been Pwned. The service answers with every leaked hash that starts the same way, padded with dummy ones, and the comparison happens on your device, so the service cannot tell which password you asked about.
Passwords it finds lead the list on the
, with how many times each was seen.
Under
Your email addresses
, each address used in your items can be checked with one of three services:

items.s: LeakCheck
names the services an address appeared in. The address goes to LeakCheck.
Have I Been Pwned
needs an API key of your own. The address and the key go to Have I Been Pwned.
Passwords in COMB
asks Proxynova about the address, then compares the passwords it lists with your own, on your device. Only yes or no comes out: the leaked text is never shown or kept.

runs.s: After you import a vault, and again from time to time.
It needs network features to be allowed.
Results are kept in memory only, so they are gone once the vault locks. Run the check again to see them.
A check finds only leaks the service knows about. A password it does not find can still be weak or reused.

topics.title: Places for copies

runs.s: A place is somewhere outside this device where WM Pass keeps copies of your encrypted vault: a folder, a cloud account, a server or a mailbox. The same places serve backups, file sync and shared vaults.
A vault kept on one device is lost with it. A copy somewhere else is how you get it back, and because only the encrypted file goes there, the place cannot read it.
Add one under Settings, Backups or Settings, Sync and accounts, with
Add a place
. Places come in four groups:

items.s: A folder on this phone, which can be one that a cloud app or Syncthing carries on from there.

Accounts. With Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive and Box you sign in on the service's own page in your browser, and WM Pass never sees that password. With pCloud, MEGA, iCloud Drive and Proton Drive you sign in inside WM Pass.

Servers and storage, which covers WebDAV, S3, SFTP, FTP, SMB, NFS, and Synology or QNAP NAS boxes. WebDAV and S3 fill in the address for many services, such as Nextcloud, Backblaze B2 or Cloudflare R2.
Somewhere else, which means a Git repository on GitHub, GitLab or Gitea, or a mailbox over IMAP.

runs.s: What WM Pass needs to reach a place is kept on this phone under a key in its secure hardware, not in the vault, so scheduled backups can run while the vault is locked. For pCloud, MEGA and Proton Drive it keeps only the session the sign-in hands back.
Each backup is written, read back and compared before any older copy is removed, so a failed run can leave one copy too many, never one too few.
Set up at least one place before you rely on the vault. A lost device with no backup is a lost vault.
A place on a server needs network features to be allowed, and adding one allows them.
Some kinds can send a password across the network as text if you let them: plain FTP, IMAP without TLS, and NFS without Kerberos. The dialog says so where it applies.
A public Git repository lets anyone download the encrypted file, so WM Pass refuses one unless you allow it.
An SFTP server's key, and a NAS's own certificate if you accept it, are remembered on the first connection. If either changes later, WM Pass refuses to connect.
Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive and Box appear only in builds that were registered with each service.

topics.title: Keeping devices in sync

runs.s: Sync keeps the same vault on several devices. Changes made on any of them meet up and merge, so nothing typed on one device is lost on another.
Copies of a vault on several devices drift apart as you edit. Sync brings them together without one overwriting another.
There are three ways, and you can use more than one:

items.s: Through a folder or server. Turn on sync for any
place
under Settings, Sync and accounts. Each device leaves its own encrypted copy there and merges everyone else's. A device only ever writes its own file, so two syncing at once cannot undo each other.
On your own network, where two paired devices talk directly. See
Through an account, when a Bitwarden, Vaultwarden or WM Pass server account syncs with its server. See

runs.s: Merging goes field by field, and the newest value of each field wins. If two devices changed the same password, the value that loses goes into that item's history, so a conflict never destroys a password.
File sync runs about 20 seconds after you change something, so a burst of edits makes one trip, and whenever you choose
Sync now
. Attachments are carried across once each, already encrypted.
Pick whichever your devices can all reach.
File sync runs for the vault you opened at the door, not inside a nested vault or an account.
A file at the same place that is under another key, such as someone else's vault, is left alone.
Merging an older copy is harmless: newer values still win.

topics.title: Syncing over your own network

runs.s: Two of your devices on the same network can sync directly, with no server or cloud in between. You pair them once, and after that either can start a sync.
Some people want their vault on a phone and a computer without it ever touching someone else's server.
Pair under Settings, Sync and accounts, with
Pair a device
. Either scan a code that the other device shows, or compare six digits on both screens and accept on both.

A shown code holds a one-off secret and stops working after two minutes. Six digits work without a camera: each side commits to its part before seeing the other's, so someone in the middle gets one chance in a million, and a failed try shows on both screens.
Pairing stores the other device's public key, and later connections from any other key are refused.
To sync, tap
Wait for one
on one device and
Sync now
on the other. Before anything is sent, each side proves it holds the vault's key, so a paired device with another vault, or one still on the key from before a
rekey
, gets nothing.
They swap only the items that differ, and merge them as file sync does. An attachment goes across only if the vault refers to it and the other side asked for it.
When your devices are often on the same Wi-Fi and you would rather not use a cloud account.
It counts as network use, so network features must be allowed.
Devices find each other by an advert that names nothing. A device that connects can still learn this one's public key, a fixed identifier on that network that opens nothing.
A device you forget needs pairing again before it can sync.

topics.title: Bitwarden and KeePass accounts

runs.s: WM Pass can open a vault that lives somewhere else: a KeePass file where it is, or an account on Bitwarden, Vaultwarden or a WM Pass server. It opens in place of your own vault, in the same screens.
Moving everything at once is not always possible. A work account on a Bitwarden server, or a KeePass file shared with others, can stay where it is while you use WM Pass for it.
Add one under Settings, Sync and accounts, with
Add an account
, or at the door. Choose Bitwarden, a server of your own, or a KeePass file.
It then appears at the door beside your own vault. Choose it there and type its own password.

For a server account, your password is never sent: a key made from it proves who you are, as with any Bitwarden app. The first sign-in from a new device may need a code Bitwarden emails you, or a two-step code, typed beside the password.
Changes go up to the server after each edit. If it cannot be reached they wait, and WM Pass keeps an offline copy, encrypted as the server's is.
A KeePass file stays where it is, and WM Pass writes back to it on each save, keeping one earlier copy beside its own files. Syncthing or a cloud app can carry the file.
For a vault you share with people who use Bitwarden or KeePass, or one an employer runs.
Bitwarden does not publish its API, so a change on its side can stop this working.
A KeePass file is only as strong as its own settings. WM Pass writes it with an experimental KDBX 4 writer, so it reads every save back and compares it, and keeps the previous file.
Inside an account, Settings, Security leaves out the master password, ways in, duress and emergency groups. Those belong to a WM Pass vault.
Removing an account forgets it on this device, with its offline copy. Nothing on the server or in the file changes.

topics.title: Vaults inside a vault

runs.s: A vault can hold other vaults: nested ones, kept apart for your own use, and shared ones, which you and other people each open with your own key.
Some passwords belong to one part of your life, such as work, or to a group, such as a family. A separate vault keeps them apart, and a shared one lets several people keep the same logins up to date.
Both are under Settings, Sync and accounts, Nested and shared vaults.
A nested vault
is its own encrypted file, made with its own password. It opens from inside this vault without asking again.
A shared vault
lives at a
place
that everyone sharing it can reach, such as a cloud folder. Each person has their own key to it, so nobody needs anyone else's password.
To join someone's shared vault, choose
Join someone's shared vault

and make a code to send them. Read the short fingerprint it shows out to them, so they can check nobody swapped the code. Their invitation comes back to the same list, where you accept it and pick the place.
The owner adds people from
People
by pasting their code, once the fingerprint they read out matches. Removing someone moves the vault to a new key, so they cannot open anything written from then on.
Open one from the list and it works like your own vault. To leave, lock, or come back to this page and choose the row under
You are inside
A nested vault for a part of your life you want kept apart. A shared vault for family or a team, without a server.
Anyone who can open the outer vault can open a nested one too, since it opens without asking again.
Everyone with the key to a shared vault can read and change everything in it. Someone you remove keeps any copy they already had, so change the passwords they could see.
Inside a nested or shared vault, Settings, Security shows only the locking choices. Ways in, duress and the emergency kit belong to the vault you opened at the door.

topics.title: Moving passwords in and out

runs.s: Import brings items in from another password manager or authenticator app. Export writes your vault out again, encrypted or as plain text.
Your passwords should never be stuck in one app, this one included.
Under Settings, Import, choose your old app's export file. WM Pass shows how many items it found, a few of their names, and any it could not read, before anything is added.

Password managers: 1Password, Apple Passwords, Avast, Avira, Bitwarden, Buttercup, Chrome and other Chromium browsers, Dashlane, Enpass, Firefox, Kaspersky, KeePass and KeePassXC, Keeper, LastPass, mSecure, NordPass, Password Safe, Proton Pass, Psono, RoboForm, SafeInCloud, Sticky Password and Zoho Vault. Authenticators: Aegis, 2FAS, andOTP, Authenticator Pro, Bitwarden Authenticator, Ente Auth, FreeOTP+, LastPass Authenticator, Proton Authenticator and Raivo. For Google Authenticator, tap
Scan Google Authenticator's code
and scan each of its export codes in turn.
A file with a password, such as a KeePass or SafeInCloud database, asks for it first. Items already in the vault are skipped, and the result says how many.
Under Settings, Export, a
WM Pass vault
or a
KeePass database
stays encrypted.
Bitwarden JSON
CSV
and a
Printable page
are plain text that anyone who opens them can read.
